titleText.es: Hasta ahora estoy contento con mi Kindle 2, pero si cortan el acceso gratuito a la Wikipedia, pienso plantarme en el césped de Jeff Bezos borracho y negándome a irme.
titleText.en: I'm happy with my Kindle 2 so far, but if they cut off the free Wikipedia browsing, I plan to show up drunk on Jeff Bezos's lawn and refuse to leave.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive closely translates the official title text. Kindle, Wikipedia, and Jeff Bezos are proper names in this metadata rather than comic-image vocabulary targets.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: e-books; electronic books
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Ebook is an English loan used in Spanish for a book read on an electronic device. The printed plural ebooks adds -s.

example.en: I read e-books on the train.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: huh?; eh? (a skeptical or surprised echo)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Eh can repeat or react to what was just said. The questioning tone can show surprise, doubt, or mild skepticism rather than hesitation.

example.en: You're leaving tomorrow, huh?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: idiots; imbeciles (plural insult)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Imbécil can describe a person as very foolish and is normally insulting. The plural imbéciles carries a written accent.

example.en: Don't call them idiots.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: for what purpose; what for (before qué)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In para qué, para asks about the goal or use of something. Qué keeps its written accent because it is asking a question.

example.en: What is this key for?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: mobile; available through a mobile device or network
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Here móvil is an adjective describing a kind of access, not the noun used in Spain for a cell phone. It has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: The app offers mobile access.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to; introduces the place, service, or resource being accessed
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Acceso is normally followed by a before the thing that someone can reach or use: acceso a internet, acceso al edificio. A and el combine as al.

example.en: We have access to the library.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: web; internet
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Web is an English loan commonly used as a feminine noun in Spanish, as in la web. It can refer to the World Wide Web or to a website, depending on context.

example.es: Encontré la información en la web.
example.en: I found the information on the web.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: free; at no cost
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Gratis does not change for gender or number.

example.en: Admission is free.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I spend; I may spend (a length of time)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With me, pase comes from pasarse and describes spending time in a state or activity. The ordinary present form paso changes to pase after a trigger such as aunque when the situation is treated as uncertain rather than stated as fact.

example.es: Aunque me pase una semana enfermo, terminaré el trabajo.
example.en: Even if I spend a week sick, I will finish the work.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: a penny; any money (in sin blanca)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: A blanca was an old coin. In the fixed informal expression sin blanca, the word now contributes the idea of not having even the smallest amount of money.

example.en: I got home without a penny.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: city
to find out; to learn about something
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Enterarme joins the dictionary form enterar with me. In this pronominal use, enterarse de means to become informed or find something out; it does not mean to put something inside.

example.en: I want to find out about the news.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word here; required after enterarse before the information
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish uses enterarse de before the fact, news, or subject learned. The de remains even when natural English uses only find out.

example.en: She found out about the change.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: sounds familiar; rings a bell
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Suena is a present form of sonar. With me, te, le, nos, os, or les, it can say that a name, idea, or thing feels familiar to someone.

example.en: That name sounds familiar to me.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: give me (informal singular command)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dame joins da, the positive command of dar for one familiar listener, with me for the recipient. Positive commands attach short words such as me to the end.

example.en: Give me a minute.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: scratch; scrape (informal singular command)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Rasca is the positive command of rascar for one familiar listener. It has the same written form as the ordinary present form used with él or ella.

example.en: Scratch the label carefully.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: hitchhiker
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Autoestopista names a person who travels by getting free rides from passing vehicles. The same noun form can refer to a man or a woman.

example.es: El conductor recogió a una autoestopista.
example.en: The driver picked up a hitchhiker.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: galactic (masculine singular)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Galáctico describes something related to a galaxy. The feminine form is galáctica, and the plural forms are galácticos and galácticas.

example.en: They imagined a galactic journey.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you connect acceso to the place, service, or resource that can be reached or used?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use acceso followed by a, then name the place, service, or resource.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by,” and recurso means the thing available for use. Keep a after acceso: acceso a internet, acceso a la cuenta, or acceso al edificio. Al is the combined form of a + el.

example.es: Los estudiantes tienen acceso al laboratorio.
example.en: The students have access to the laboratory.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: aunque + presente de subjuntivo para una posibilidad incierta
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say “even if” when the condition is possible but not being stated as a fact?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use aunque, then put the uncertain action in its special subjunctive form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” The subjunctive is a special verb form used when the speaker does not present the condition as an established fact. For example, ordinary llueve becomes llueva, and paso can become pase. Use an ordinary form after aunque when you mean “although” and treat the event as a fact.

example.en: Even if it rains, we will go out.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone spends a length of time in a certain state?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching form of pasarse, state the duration, then add the word describing the person's condition.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus signs mean “followed by,” período means the length of time, and estado means the condition. Pasarse uses me, te, se, nos, or os to match the person; only the verb changes for time and person. A describing adjective also matches that person when its form changes.

example.es: Ana se pasó dos días enferma.
example.en: Ana spent two days sick.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What informal Spanish expression says that someone has no money at all?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use sin blanca to mean “without a penny” or “completely broke.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is a fixed colloquial expression, especially associated with Spain. A blanca was once a low-value coin, so the expression pictures someone as lacking even the smallest amount of money. Do not change blanca to match the person.

example.es: Después del viaje se quedó sin blanca.
example.en: After the trip, he was completely broke.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone finds out about or learns something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching form of enterarse, then de, then state the information or subject learned.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” Enterarse is used with a short person marker: me entero, te enteras, se entera, nos enteramos, os enteráis, or se enteran. Keep de before the fact, news, event, or topic, even where English simply says find out.

example.es: Nos enteramos de la noticia ayer.
example.en: We found out about the news yesterday.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something sounds familiar to someone?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Name the thing, use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person, then use the matching form of sonar.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus signs mean “used together,” algo stands for the familiar thing, and the slash marks a choice among the short person words. The thing controls the verb: ese nombre me suena, but esos nombres me suenan. Spanish can also put the thing after the verb.

example.en: That song sounds familiar to me.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: The scratched device reveals a reference to The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Douglas Adams's science-fiction series features an electronic guide containing vast amounts of useful travel information. A wirelessly connected e-reader resembles that fictional guide, so scratching away the Kindle branding uncovers the joke's imagined true identity.

applications.explanationEn: Acceso names availability, a introduces the resource, and la web fills that resource slot; móvil only describes the kind of access.
Acceso names the thing first, and móvil follows it as the neutral description.
Móvil stays singular to match acceso and has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.
Aunque presents a possible concession, me belongs to the pronominal verb, and pase is the special uncertain form rather than ordinary paso.

applications.exampleEs: ME PASE MESES BORRACHO Y SIN BLANCA
applications.explanationEn: Me and pase form pasarse for the speaker, meses supplies the duration, and borracho and sin blanca supply two coordinated conditions.
Sin and blanca form the fixed informal money expression; blanca remains feminine singular as part of the idiom.
Ciudad names the place first, and extraña follows it as the neutral description.
Extraña uses its feminine singular form to match the feminine singular noun ciudad.
Podré is poder's first-person future form: the irregular future base podr- takes the ending -é for the speaker.
Podré changes for the speaker and future time, while seguir stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the action made possible.
Seguir supplies the idea of continuing, and usando is usar's ongoing -ando form.
Para introduces the purpose, and enterarme keeps enterar in its unchanged dictionary form with me attached.
Enterar remains in its unchanged dictionary form, and me is attached directly to its end to match the speaker.

applications.exampleEs: ENTERARME DE TODO LO QUE NECESITO
applications.explanationEn: Enterarme gives the speaker's form, de introduces what is learned, and todo lo que necesito fills the information slot.
Lo and que work together to introduce an unnamed thing rather than a masculine noun.
